title: 07. Concurrency: Process vs Thread — The Big Picture
summary: Process vs Thread — The Big Picture: explanations and runnable examples.

sections.title: Explanation (Junior Developer Style)
sections.body:
Imagine you work in an **office building**.

### 🏢 Process = Entire Office Floor
- Each **process** is like a **separate office floor** in a building.
- Every floor has its **own rooms, furniture, electricity, staff** — completely **independent**.
- If floor 1 catches fire, floor 2 is **NOT affected**.
- Floors **don't share** resources. To send something from floor 1 to floor 2, you need to use a **messenger** (Inter-Process Communication).

### 👷 Thread = Employee on That Floor
- A **thread** is like an **employee** working on that floor.
- Multiple employees (threads) **share the same rooms, printers, coffee machine** (memory) on the same floor.
- They work **together** on the same tasks.
- If one employee makes a mess in the shared kitchen — **everyone is affected**.

### 🔑 Key Technical Differences

| Feature | Process | Thread |
|---|---|---|
| Memory | Own separate memory space | Shared memory within process |
| Creation Cost | Heavy (slow to create) | Light (fast to create) |
| Communication | Complex (IPC — Pipes, Queues) | Easy (shared memory) |
| Crash Impact | One crash doesn't affect others | One crash can kill all threads |
| CPU Cores | Can use multiple cores | Limited by GIL in Python |
| Data Sharing | No sharing by default | Shares data easily |
| Overhead | High | Low |
| Isolation | Fully isolated | Not isolated |

### 🏗️ How Python Creates Them

```
Your Python Script (Main Process)
│
├── spawns → Process 1 (separate memory, separate Python interpreter)
│               └── Thread A (inside Process 1)
│               └── Thread B (inside Process 1)
│
├── spawns → Process 2 (separate memory, separate Python interpreter)
│               └── Thread C (inside Process 2)
│
└── Main Thread (inside Main Process)
        └── Thread D
        └── Thread E
```

sections.title: 5 Examples
sections.body:
### Example 1: Seeing Process ID vs Thread ID

```python
import os
import threading
import multiprocessing

def show_thread_info():
    print(f"  Thread Name: {threading.current_thread().name}")
    print(f"  Thread ID:   {threading.get_ident()}")
    print(f"  Process ID:  {os.getpid()}")   # Same PID for all threads!

def show_process_info():
    print(f"  Process ID:  {os.getpid()}")   # Different PID for each process!
    print(f"  Parent PID:  {os.getppid()}")
    print(f"  Thread ID:   {threading.get_ident()}")

print("=" * 50)
print("THREADING DEMO — Same Process, Different Threads")
print("=" * 50)

t1 = threading.Thread(target=show_thread_info, name="Thread-Alpha")
t2 = threading.Thread(target=show_thread_info, name="Thread-Beta")

t1.start(); t1.join()
t2.start(); t2.join()

print("\n" + "=" * 50)
print("MULTIPROCESSING DEMO — Different Processes")
print("=" * 50)

p1 = multiprocessing.Process(target=show_process_info)
p2 = multiprocessing.Process(target=show_process_info)

p1.start(); p1.join()
p2.start(); p2.join()

# OUTPUT:
# THREADING DEMO — Same Process, Different Threads
#   Thread Name: Thread-Alpha
#   Thread ID:   140234567890  ← Different
#   Process ID:  12345          ← SAME! Both threads in same process
#
#   Thread Name: Thread-Beta
#   Thread ID:   140234567999  ← Different
#   Process ID:  12345          ← SAME!
#
# MULTIPROCESSING DEMO — Different Processes
#   Process ID:  12346  ← Different from main (12345)
#   Process ID:  12347  ← Different from main AND from p1
```

### Example 2: Memory IS Shared in Threads, NOT in Processes

```python
import threading
import multiprocessing

# ──────────────────────────────────────────
# THREAD DEMO: Threads SHARE memory
# ──────────────────────────────────────────
shared_list = []  # This list is SHARED among threads

def thread_add_item(item):
    shared_list.append(item)
    print(f"Thread added '{item}'. List is now: {shared_list}")

t1 = threading.Thread(target=thread_add_item, args=("Apple",))
t2 = threading.Thread(target=thread_add_item, args=("Banana",))

t1.start(); t1.join()
t2.start(); t2.join()

print(f"Final shared_list in MAIN: {shared_list}")
# OUTPUT: ['Apple', 'Banana']  ✅ Threads modified the SAME list!

print("\n" + "─" * 50)

# ──────────────────────────────────────────
# PROCESS DEMO: Processes do NOT share memory
# ──────────────────────────────────────────
process_list = []  # Each process gets its OWN COPY

def process_add_item(item):
    process_list.append(item)
    print(f"Process added '{item}'. Its local list: {process_list}")
    # This process has its OWN copy of process_list!

p1 = multiprocessing.Process(target=process_add_item, args=("Apple",))
p2 = multiprocessing.Process(target=process_add_item, args=("Banana",))

p1.start(); p1.join()
p2.start(); p2.join()

print(f"Final process_list in MAIN: {process_list}")
# OUTPUT: []  ❌ Main process list is UNCHANGED!
# Each process modified its OWN private copy
```

### Example 3: Creation Time — Thread is Faster to Create

```python
import threading
import multiprocessing
import time

def do_nothing():
    pass  # Just an empty function

# Measure time to create 100 THREADS
start = time.time()
threads = []
for _ in range(100):
    t = threading.Thread(target=do_nothing)
    threads.append(t)
    t.start()

for t in threads:
    t.join()

thread_time = time.time() - start
print(f"Time to create & run 100 THREADS:    {thread_time:.4f} seconds")

# Measure time to create 100 PROCESSES
start = time.time()
processes = []
for _ in range(100):
    p = multiprocessing.Process(target=do_nothing)
    processes.append(p)
    p.start()

for p in processes:
    p.join()

process_time = time.time() - start
print(f"Time to create & run 100 PROCESSES:  {process_time:.4f} seconds")

print(f"\nProcesses are {process_time/thread_time:.1f}x SLOWER to create than Threads!")

# Typical OUTPUT:
# Time to create & run 100 THREADS:    0.0123 seconds
# Time to create & run 100 PROCESSES:  1.2456 seconds
# Processes are ~100x SLOWER to create than Threads!
```

### Example 4: Crash Isolation — Process Crash vs Thread Crash

```python
import threading
import multiprocessing
import time

# ──────────────────────────────────────────
# THREAD CRASH: Affects the whole program (sort of)
# ──────────────────────────────────────────
def good_thread_worker():
    for i in range(5):
        print(f"  Good thread working... step {i}")
        time.sleep(0.5)

def bad_thread_worker():
    time.sleep(1)
    raise Exception("💥 Thread crashed!")  # This will print error but others continue

print("=== THREAD CRASH DEMO ===")
t1 = threading.Thread(target=good_thread_worker, name="GoodThread")
t2 = threading.Thread(target=bad_thread_worker, name="BadThread")

t1.start()
t2.start()
t1.join()
t2.join()
print("Main thread continues after thread crash\n")

# ──────────────────────────────────────────
# PROCESS CRASH: Other processes are SAFE
# ──────────────────────────────────────────
def good_process_worker():
    for i in range(5):
        print(f"  Good process working... step {i}")
        time.sleep(0.5)

def bad_process_worker():
    time.sleep(1)
    raise Exception("💥 Process crashed!")

print("=== PROCESS CRASH DEMO ===")
p1 = multiprocessing.Process(target=good_process_worker)
p2 = multiprocessing.Process(target=bad_process_worker)

p1.start()
p2.start()
p1.join()
p2.join()

print(f"p1 exit code: {p1.exitcode}")  # 0 = success
print(f"p2 exit code: {p2.exitcode}")  # 1 = crashed
print("Main process still running! p1 was unaffected by p2's crash.")
```

### Example 5: Real World — When to Use Thread vs Process

```python
import threading
import multiprocessing
import time
import requests  # pip install requests

# ──────────────────────────────────────────
# USE CASE 1: I/O Bound → USE THREADING
# Example: Download multiple files simultaneously
# ──────────────────────────────────────────

urls = [
    "https://httpbin.org/delay/1",
    "https://httpbin.org/delay/1",
    "https://httpbin.org/delay/1",
]

def download_url(url):
    print(f"  Downloading {url}...")
    # response = requests.get(url)  # In real code, uncomment this
    time.sleep(1)  # Simulating network delay
    print(f"  ✅ Done: {url}")

print("=== I/O BOUND TASK: Downloading URLs ===")
start = time.time()

# Without threading: 3 seconds (1 sec each, sequential)
# With threading:   ~1 second (all run simultaneously)
threads = [threading.Thread(target=download_url, args=(url,)) for url in urls]
[t.start() for t in threads]
[t.join() for t in threads]
print(f"Threading download time: {time.time()-start:.2f}s\n")

# ──────────────────────────────────────────
# USE CASE 2: CPU Bound → USE MULTIPROCESSING
# Example: Calculate factorial of large numbers
# ──────────────────────────────────────────

def cpu_heavy_task(n):
    """Calculate sum of squares — CPU intensive"""
    result = sum(i * i for i in range(n))
    print(f"  Computed sum of squares for n={n}: {result}")
    return result

numbers = [5_000_000, 5_000_000, 5_000_000]

print("=== CPU BOUND TASK: Heavy Calculations ===")
start = time.time()
processes = [multiprocessing.Process(target=cpu_heavy_task, args=(n,)) for n in numbers]
[p.start() for p in processes]
[p.join() for p in processes]
print(f"Multiprocessing compute time: {time.time()-start:.2f}s")
# Runs TRULY in parallel on multiple CPU cores!
```

quiz.question: What is the difference between a Process and a Thread?
options: ALL waiting threads are woken up simultaneously — this is one of Event's key properties.
The simple rule: CPU-bound → multiprocessing, I/O-bound → threading. > > Use multiprocessing when: > - Task requires significant CPU computation (data crunching, image…
Python's multiprocessing provides several IPC mechanisms: > > 1.
A process is an independent program in execution with its own memory space, file handles, and system resources.
quiz.explanation: A process is an independent program in execution with its own memory space, file handles, and system resources. The OS treats each process as a completely isolated unit. A thread, on the other hand, is a lightweight unit of execution that lives inside a process and shares the process's memory and resources with other threads in the same process.

quiz.question: Why is memory isolation important in processes?
options: Two approaches: > > Approach 1: as_completed(timeout=N) — process results that finish within N seconds total: > python > from concurrent.futures import as_completed,…
get(timeout=5) returns an item if one becomes available within 5 seconds — it's time-bounded blocking.
This is a serious bug. Making all threads daemon means any ongoing work can be killed mid-execution when the program exits.
Memory isolation is critical for safety and reliability. In my experience working on payment processing services, we ran each payment gateway integration as a separate process.
quiz.explanation: Memory isolation is critical for safety and reliability. In my experience working on payment processing services, we ran each payment gateway integration as a separate process. If one gateway's code had a memory leak or a bug that corrupted its data, it could never affect the other gateways or the main application.

quiz.question: What is IPC (Inter-Process Communication) and why do we need it?
options: Memory isolation is critical for safety and reliability. In my experience working on payment processing services, we ran each payment gateway integration as a separate process.
Several strategies: > > 1. multiprocessing module — Each process has its own GIL, so N processes = N truly parallel Python interpreters.
By default, if a thread raises an unhandled exception, Python prints the traceback but the thread just dies silently — the main thread doesn't know about it!
Since processes have isolated memory, they can't just read each other's variables.
quiz.explanation: Since processes have isolated memory, they can't just read each other's variables. IPC is the set of mechanisms that allows processes to exchange data. Python's multiprocessing module provides: Pipe (one-to-one, like a telephone line), Queue (many-to-many, like a shared inbox), shared Value/Array (shared memory variables), and Manager objects (complex shared data structures like dicts and lists).

In CPython (the standard Python interpreter), the answer is effectively no for CPU-bound tasks, because of the GIL — Global Interpreter Lock.
quiz.explanation: In CPython (the standard Python interpreter), the answer is effectively no for CPU-bound tasks, because of the GIL — Global Interpreter Lock. The GIL is a mutex that allows only one thread to execute Python bytecode at a time. So even if you have 8 cores, only 1 thread runs Python code at any moment.

If you mark a thread as a daemon thread, the main process will kill it abruptly when the main program exits, regardless of whether it finished its work. This distinction is important in production code.
